title: Security review - Encryption/KMS/BYOK/HSM (Marlin Payments)
summary: Review of Redwood encryption at rest and in transit, KMS/BYOK options, HSM support, key rotation and audit log capabilities. Customer (Marlin Payments) requires FIPS/HSM-backed keys for production, SOC 2 proof, RBAC/SSO integration, and data residency constraints in eu-west-1. Agreed next steps: send SOC 2 report and KMS/architecture doc, schedule follow-up for BYOK pilot and legal review.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Ethan Morris (Redwood SA); James Liu (Marlin CISO), Priya Desai (Head Cloud Ops), Liam O'Connor (DevOps), Maya Patel (Legal)

Auto-summary: quick security review focused on encryption at rest/in-transit and key management. Customer wants BYOK with HSM-backed keys, proof of SOC 2 and audit log retention, plus RBAC/SSO integration notes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll run through encryption and KMS options today — try to leave time for questions. James, Maya from legal are you on?
[00:12] James (Marlin): Yeah I'm here. Hi. Priya and Liam too. Thanks, Alex.
[00:18] Priya (Marlin): Hi, thanks. We're particularly interested in how Redwood handles keys for production workloads and any HSM support.
[00:26] Sofia (Redwood): Great, that's exactly what we'll cover — at rest encryption, TLS in transit, KMS options, and BYOK / HSM specifics. I'll kick off with a high-level and Ethan can do the architecture deep dive.
[00:35] Ethan (Redwood): Quick note — some transcriptions sometimes say KV cash. We actually mean KV cache and KV cache encryption relates to token caching but won’t get too deep unless you'd like.
[00:45] James: Yep, KV cache is fine. Our big item: we need FIPS 140-2/3 HSM-backed keys for any customer PII models in production. Can you support that?
[00:58] Sofia: Short answer yes; Redwood supports BYOK via cloud KMS integrations and can integrate with HSM-backed KMS (AWS KMS with CloudHSM, GCP CMEK with HSM, or customer-managed HSM). We have customers using both cloud HSM and external HSMs.
[01:15] Priya: So practically, how does that look — do you import keys, or do we provision them in our tenant KMS and Redwood calls them? We need to avoid key material leaving our control.
[01:28] Alex: Good question. We support Bring Your Own Key where the key material stays in your KMS — Redwood never sees raw key material. The service uses KMS APIs to perform envelope encryption; the data encryption keys (DEKs) are wrapped/unwrapped in your KMS.
[01:43] James: So Redwood stores only ciphertext and the wrapped DEK?
[01:47] Sofia: Right. We store ciphertext and metadata — the wrapped keys are not usable outside your KMS. Redwood only has the ability to request decryption via the KMS service, assuming IAM permissions are granted.
[01:58] Liam: What about ephemeral instances and cross-region replication? We have DR in eu-west-1 and sometimes replicate to us-east-1 for warm failover. Keys can't leave eu-west-1 for regulatory reasons.
[02:12] Ethan: We support regional key scoping. For compliance you can choose region-scoped keys and restrict Redwood to call KMS endpoints in eu-west-1. For cross-region failover, we typically recommend a key in each region and rotation/replication handled by your KMS replication tools. We'll document recommended patterns.
[02:30] Priya: Great. What's the latency impact of calling customer KMS on inference path? We do per-request decryption? That could add milliseconds per call.
[02:40] Sofia: We use envelope encryption and cache DEKs in a secure cache (in-memory) for the serving runtime. The expensive KMS unwrap happens infrequently — on key rotation or initial session. Typical added latency after warm-up is low, but there is a small cold-start cost we can quantify in a pilot.
[02:58] James: Sounds ok, but we need numbers. We'll want to run benchmarks with our PII payloads.
[03:05] Alex: Absolutely. We'll propose a BYOK pilot that includes latency and throughput benchmarks with your KMS. We'll also include a runbook for failure modes — e.g., KMS API throttling or network partition — and fallback behaviors.
[03:20] Maya (Marlin Legal): On the legal side we need clarity on key custody, access controls, and auditability. Do you provide audit logs showing when a decrypt call was made and by which Redwood service principal?
[03:33] Ethan: Yes — we have detailed audit logs for all KMS operations initiated by Redwood: timestamp, resource, Redwood principal, and request ID. Those logs are retained per customer config — we can push them to your logging endpoint or provide access via console.
[03:47] Priya: Retention windows matter — can we get logs exported to our SIEM and S3 for at least 7 years? Some regs require long retention.
[03:57] Sofia: We can support log forwarding to your SIEM or S3. Seven years is long but technically possible; we'll surface any cost implications. Typically we support 90/365 day retention in console and export hooks for longer-term archival.
[04:13] James: Another item — separation of duties. We need to ensure only authorized Redwood service principals can call decrypt and that we can rotate keys without downtime.
[04:24] Alex: You'll manage IAM roles on your KMS side. Redwood will request a limited-role that can Decrypt/GenerateDataKey only, and we recommend short-lived credentials. For rotation, we can do rolling unwraps and cache population to avoid downtime.
[04:39] Liam: Does Redwood support HSM-backed key attestation or attestation proofs? We use CloudHSM and need attestation for key provenance.
[04:49] Ethan: For HSMs like AWS CloudHSM we can surface CloudHSM cluster IDs and show that KMS keys are backed by HSM. We can provide architecture diagrams and attestations from the cloud provider. For on-prem HSMs we typically do a connector model and can support PKCS#11 integration — we'll send details.
[05:05] Priya: Regarding network, all traffic must be TLS 1.2/1.3 and we require mTLS to the VPC endpoints. Is that supported?
[05:12] Sofia: Yes, in Private deployments we support private connectivity with mTLS and mutual peering; for hosted we use TLS 1.2/1.3 and recommend VPC endpoints/PrivateLink where available. We can discuss per-deployment.
[05:27] James: Do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs? We need to see the reports and the auditor's scope.
[05:34] Alex: We have SOC 2 Type II and are ISO-aligned. I'll send the SOC 2 package after this call.
[05:40] Maya: Also need DPA and specifics on subprocessors and where data is stored.
[05:45] Alex: We'll attach sample DPA and subprocessor list; we can take redlines.
[05:50] Priya: One more technical: tokenization and trimming of logs. We need audit logs but must ensure PII is not written to plaintext in logs. How does Redwood handle sensitive fields?
[06:02] Sofia: We support configurable scrubbing and redaction pipelines. By default, system logs avoid PII; request/response logs can be configured to be redacted before storage. We also support per-route policies to disable request logging for sensitive routes.
[06:18] Liam: Good. For the pilot we'll want a sandbox where we can test with masked PII.
[06:24] Alex: We'll provision a sandbox with sampling enabled and masked payloads.
[06:28] James: Back to keys — what's the lifecycle for rotation? We have quarterly rotation requirements.
[06:35] Ethan: Key rotation can be managed entirely within your KMS. We recommend rotating DEKs frequently and using KMS to rewrap. Redwood will fetch the new wrapped DEK and rotate caches. We can support automated rotation workflows triggered by KMS or via Redwood schedule integration.
[06:51] Priya: If KMS access is lost, do you have a fallback? For example, if our KMS endpoint is temporarily unavailable, can Redwood serve cached sessions to avoid downtime?
[07:02] Sofia: Yes, with controlled cache TTLs. We can serve using cached DEKs for a configurable short period. For longer outages we have fallback routing to a warm standby region or fallback model variants that don't use PII — but that depends on your risk tolerance.
[07:18] James: Ok. Let's talk about HSM for BYOK — we require FIPS 140-2 level 3 if possible. Is that supported?
[07:26] Ethan: Support depends on provider. Cloud HSM offerings can meet FIPS levels depending on configuration; for on-prem HSM we can integrate with FIPS 140-2/3 hardware. We'll include guidance and required certs from providers in the doc pack.
[07:43] Maya: What KMS vendors have you integrated with? We need to ensure compatibility with our existing HashiCorp Vault deployment.
[07:51] Sofia: We have integrations for AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault (transit), and on-prem PKCS#11 HSMs. For Vault transit, we use an authenticated connector pattern and don't store keys in Redwood.
[08:05] Priya: Can you give a quick overview of the flow for HashiCorp Vault transit?
[08:11] Ethan: Sure — Redwood will call the Vault Transit API to encrypt/decrypt DEKs. We recommend a connector running in your environment that holds Vault tokens and exposes an internal endpoint to Redwood; that way root tokens never leave your control. We'll sketch the architecture and provide a sample connector image.
[08:30] Alex: (brief interruption) There's a question in chat about token limits and rate limiting for KMS calls.
[08:36] Liam: Oh yeah — KMS API limits can be a problem at scale. What's your recommended throttling strategy?
[08:42] Sofia: We do adaptive batching and caching; for DEK operations we batch generation during session start. For high throughput we'll recommend using per-host DEKs and reuse them for short-lived sessions to reduce KMS calls. Also, the pilot will measure KMS call RPS and help configure backoff/retry windows.
[08:59] James: We also want to ensure RBAC/SSO integration — can Redwood integrate with our Okta and provide role-based access to the console and APIs?
[09:09] Alex: Yes, we support SAML/SSO (Okta, Azure AD) and granular RBAC. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (admin, operator, auditor). We'll provide a guide for SSO setup.
[09:21] Priya: For auditability, can we get an immutable audit trail? Some regs require tamper-evident logs.
[09:29] Ethan: Our audit logs are append-only and can be forwarded to your immutable store (e.g., WORM S3). We can also sign logs and provide integrity checks.
[09:41] Maya: On the DPA, we have specific clauses around key ownership and scope. Will Redwood accept a clause that keys are owned and controlled by client and not accessible by Redwood?
[09:52] Alex: Yes, BYOK patterns are consistent with that clause. We'll include standard contract language used with other customers.
[09:58] James: Any limitations around model caching or partial model weights exposing data? We do not want model fine-tuning with raw customer data.
[10:07] Sofia: We do not fine-tune customer-managed models with customer data unless explicitly enabled in the settings. For hosted models we isolate training/updates and have policies to avoid data bleed. We'll include details in the security whitepaper.
[10:20] Priya: Great. One last technical — can you describe the flow end-to-end for an inference request that includes PII: request comes in, how it is encrypted at rest, how keys are used, and what is logged?
[10:31] Ethan: High level: 1) client request is TLS to Redwood (mTLS if private). 2) Request payload reaches inference runtime, we decrypt any stored payload locally using cached DEK. 3) If DEK not cached, Redwood calls your KMS to unwrap DEK. 4) Inference happens in memory, results are returned over TLS. 5) We store audit logs with no plaintext PII; logs include metadata, request IDs, and redacted fields. We'll put a sequence diagram in the doc pack.
[10:56] James: That helps.
[11:01] Alex: Any other questions from legal?
[11:05] Maya: We'll need the sample DPA and subprocessor list. Also an SLA around encryption key management.
[11:12] Alex: We'll include sample SLA language.
[11:15] Priya: Thanks, this was helpful. For the pilot, we'll want a PoC with BYOK using our Vault in eu-west-1 and a small workload. Can Redwood host the connector?
[11:26] Sofia: We can provide a reference connector image for you to run in your VPC. For managed connectors we can discuss a dedicated deploy model under Redwood Private.
[11:35] Liam: Timing — we want to execute pilot within the next two weeks. Is that realistic?
[11:40] Alex: Yes, if we get approvals and your test data and access quickly. We'll target provisioning by 2026-03-12.
[11:46] James: Ok. Can you send us the SOC 2, whitepaper, KMS architecture, and sample DPA after this?
[11:52] Alex: Yes. I'll email the docs and set up the follow-up for the week of 2026-03-15.
[11:57] Maya: We'll review DPA and get legal notes back.
[12:01] Alex: Great. Thanks everyone.

End of call.
